Let me analyze this certificate.

Certificate: R60/2000-NL1-06.02, scheme... The certificate number is "R60/2000-NL1-06.02". This is an OIML-CS certificate. Scheme A or B — not stated explicitly. NMi Certin was an Issuing Authority; these older certificates don't mention scheme. Leave scheme out or null? Rule 8: don't fabricate. Omit scheme.

project_number: 503960
page_total: 2
member_state: The Netherlands
date_issued: 2006-02-01 (1 February 2006)
oiml_issuer_id: not present.

Issuing authority: NMi Certin B.V., address lines: Hugo de Grootplein 1, 3314 EG Dordrecht, The Netherlands. Person responsible: Ing. C. Oosterman, person title: Manager Product Certification. Phone: +31 78 6332332. Email: certin@nmi.nl. Website: www.nmi.nl. oiml_issuer_id: not present.

Applicants: Laumas Elettronica S.r.l., Via Primo Maggio 6, 43030 Basilicanova (PR), ITALY.

Manufacturers: same.

Certified type: category "Load cell". Type designations: CTL. Module designation — for load cells, R60 — "Analog load cell"? Not stated; the description says "Tension, S-type load cell". Don't fabricate. module_designation: null or omit. Description: "Tension, S-type load cell"? Actually "Tension, S-type load cell" describes the load cell — tension loading, S-type. Include description.

Model family: Emax range "500 kg up to and including 10 000 kg" — that's a range, not discrete list. Number of load cell intervals varies: 2000 or 3000. Hmm. This is a range of capacities from 500 kg to 10000 kg. The table: Maximum capacity Emax = 500 kg up to and including 10000 kg (range). Accuracy class C. Maximum number of load cell intervals n = 2000 or 3000 (two values — likely corresponds to different models/variants). Y = 10000.

Is this a model matrix? n has two values: 2000, 3000. There's no explicit model names. The Emax is a range rather than discrete models. Hmm.

I could model this as: characteristics.type_level: maximum_capacity as range {min: 500, max: 10000} kg; accuracy class C; ratio_y_emax_over_vmin: 10000; max_load_cell_intervals_n: could be model_level with two variants "n=2000" and "n=3000"? Or type_level as a list? The rules say lists of values → model matrix. But with only one varying attribute and no model names, creating models named "n=2000" and "n=3000" seems plausible.

Actually wait — in many R60 certs, the different n values correspond to different Emax models. Here Emax is a continuous range. The two n columns likely refer to two variants of the load cell family. Since no model names are given, I could:

Option A: type_level maximum_capacity {min 500, max 10000} kg, n at model_level with models "n=2000" and "n=3000".

Option B: keep n as type_level with value... but two values can't be a single value. Rules say "Lists of values... is a MODEL MATRIX".

Hmm, but the two columns of n (2000, 3000) in the original table span under "Maximum number of load cell intervals" — with colspan 2 for the other rows. This suggests two variants. I'll create model_family with models {"model_id": "n=2000"} and {"model_id": "n=3000"}? That seems odd since Emax is continuous.

Alternatively, maybe treat n as model_level with models labeled "variant 1 (n=2000)" and "variant 2 (n=3000)". Hmm.

Actually, more conservative: model_family omitted? But rule says include model_family ONLY if cert covers >1 model variant. The n values suggest 2 variants. The certificate covers a range of Emax (500–10000 kg) which itself suggests many models.

I think best approach: 
- type_level: maximum_capacity {min:500, max:10000} kg; accuracy_class "C"; ratio_y_emax_over_vmin 10000 (dimensionless); apportionment factor? "Fraction: P_i = 0.7" — apportionment_factor_plc = 0.7. Temperature range -10/+40 °C → characteristic temperature_range... rules example: temperature range → value {min:-10, max:40}, unit "°C". Label: temperature_range? Typically "temperature_range" with min/max. Could also be named operating_temperature_range. I'll use temperature_range.
- model_level: max_load_cell_intervals_nlc with values for two models. Model ids: hmm. Since no names, maybe "n=2000" and "n=3000". Or since Emax range, models can't be enumerated.

Actually let me reconsider: The table shows n: 2000 and 3000 as two columns. In R60 certs, this often means the load cell family includes versions with different n. So model_level entries:

{"attribute": "max_load_cell_intervals_nlc", "unit_symbol": null, "values": [{"model": "n=2000", "value": 2000}, {"model": "n=3000", "value": 3000}]}

And model_family: {"family_name": null, "models": [{"model_id": "n=2000"}, {"model_id": "n=3000"}]}.

Hmm, but is that fabrication? The two columns genuinely exist. I think it's a fair representation. Alternatively, treat n as type_level with value being a list — not allowed per rules.

I'll go with model_family with two variants.

Footnote markers: none present.

Recommendation: id "R60", edition 2000, amendment null, scheme — not stated. accuracy_classes: ["C"].

Test reports: "N° R60/2000-NL1-06.02 that includes 40 pages" — test report id same as cert number, pages 40, role "test_report". Also description with number TC6891 — "the description with number TC6891 and the appertaining documentation folder". TC6891 is a test certificate/description number. Could include as test_reports entry with role "documentation_file"? The text: "represented by the sample or samples identified in the associated Test Report, the test certificate and the description with number TC6891 and the appertaining documentation folder". Hmm, TC6891 is the "description" number. I could include test_reports: [{id: "R60/2000-NL1-06.02", pages: 40, role: "test_report"}, {id: "TC6891", role: "documentation_file"}]. Dates not given for TC6891. I'll include both.

Revision history: none.

Footnotes: none.

Certificate number: "R60/2000-NL1-06.02". 

Characteristics labels:
- maximum_capacity: value {min:500, max:10000}, unit "kg". "500 kg up to and including 10 000 kg" → min 500 max 10000.
- accuracy_class: "C" (string value, unit null).
- max_load_cell_intervals_nlc: model_level.
- ratio_y_emax_over_vmin: 10000, dimensionless.
- apportionment_factor (p_i = 0.7): label apportionment_factor? The rules example: "Apportionment factor pLC → apportionment_factor_plc". Here it's "Fraction: P_i = 0.7" — I'll use apportionment_factor_pi? Hmm. Or apportionment_factor. Value 0.7. I'll use "apportionment_factor" since it's labeled "Fraction Pi". Actually keep close: label "apportionment_factor_pi"? The subscript is i not LC. I'll use apportionment_factor_pi... hmm, maybe simpler: "apportionment_factor". Rules canonical label examples map pLC → plc. For P_i → pi. I'll use "apportionment_factor_pi".

Hmm, actually "Fraction" — in R60 the apportionment factor is denoted pLC or p_i for multiple interval. I'll go with apportionment_factor_pi.

- temperature_range: {min:-10, max:40}, unit "°C".

unit_id: leave null unless certain. I could provide "u:degree_Celsius" for temperature — the schema example shows it. Rules: "Leave unit_id: null unless you are certain of the unitsdb ID." The example in rule 2 shows "u:degree_Celsius" as a valid ID. I'll set degree_Celsius for °C and leave others null. kg — unitsdb likely "u:kilogram". I'm fairly certain degree_Celsius exists per example. For kg I'll set null to be safe? The schema example lists unit_id examples "u:degree_Celsius" | null. I'll set degree_Celsius where applicable, null otherwise.

Model family: models: [{"model_id": "n=2000", "label": null...}] — schema: model_id, label, attributes{}. I'll include attributes maybe with n. Keep simple.

Scheme (A|B) for certificate: 2006-era NMi certificates... OIML Basic vs Abigail scheme introduced later. Not stated → omit.

certificate.date_issued: "2006-02-01". Format — probably ISO date. The schema says date_issued; I'll use "2006-02-01".
